analysis.one_liner: Lets adults 50 to 64 buy into Medicare, requires Medicare drug price negotiation, and funds cheaper coverage.
analysis.headline: Fifty House Democrats backed a Medicare buy-in for people 50-64 and Medicare drug price negotiation, but no committee ever held a hearing and it died without a vote when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let people aged 50 to 64 enroll in Medicare by paying a premium set at the program's average cost per person, with the coverage counting for Affordable Care Act tax credits. It would also direct Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices, replace insurers' losses on high-cost patients with federal reinsurance payments, and spend federal money to make coverage cheaper for low- and middle-income people. It was referred to two House committees in September 2017 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults 50 to 64, a group the individual insurance market often charges the most and serves least, gain a public option to buy into Medicare at cost with access to premium tax credits. Low- and middle-income people buying on the exchanges gain richer cost-sharing help, since the bill would appropriate whatever is needed to fund the increased subsidies. Medicare beneficiaries gain from government-negotiated drug prices, and people in expensive individual markets gain from reinsurance that holds premiums down.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare buy-in for people aged 50 to 64, with the same hospital, medical, and drug benefits as standard Medicare, at a monthly premium set to the estimated average per-person cost, adjusted by region.
Makes buy-in coverage count as a qualified health plan, so enrollees can receive premium tax credits and cost-sharing subsidies they would get on the exchanges.

Repeals the rule barring the federal government from interfering with drug makers' pricing and requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate Part D drug prices with manufacturers, with semiannual reports on the discounts achieved.
Creates an Individual Market Reinsurance Fund paying insurers 80% of claims between $50,000 and $450,000 per high-cost patient, funded by fees on participating plans, to hold down premiums.

Deepens cost-sharing reductions so that people earning 100-400% of poverty pay a smaller share of their care costs, and appropriates the sums necessary to fund it — significant at a time when the administration had moved to stop these payments.

Appropriates $500 million a year for 2018-2020 for outreach and enrollment help, prioritizing areas at risk of losing all individual-market plans, and bars insurers themselves from receiving the grants.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would bear lower negotiated prices for Medicare's Part D drugs. Private insurers would lose some customers, as 50- to 64-year-olds could shift from private plans into the Medicare buy-in, and would pay fees to fund reinsurance. Federal taxpayers would fund the richer cost-sharing subsidies, the $500 million a year outreach program, and any payments under the extended risk-corridor program if plan losses exceed gains.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers, insurers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The buy-in premium must cover the full average per-person cost and may not increase Medicare's expenditures, so coverage could still be unaffordable for many 50- to 64-year-olds, especially those with incomes too high for the tax credits.

The reinsurance fund and the reauthorized risk-corridor program direct federal support to insurers' balance sheets; extending risk corridors to 2018-2020 revives a program under which the government can owe insurers money when their losses exceed their gains.
The cost-sharing subsidy funding is open-ended — 'such sums as may be necessary' — with no dollar limit on the federal appropriation.

Moving relatively expensive older enrollees out of private plans could shrink and destabilize the individual market the bill is also trying to prop up, which is why the bill pairs the buy-in with reinsurance rather than relying on it alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core offer — a cost-based public option for a group private insurers serve badly, plus government drug price negotiation and richer subsidies — is a substantial gain for ordinary people, and the design keeps the buy-in itself budget-neutral for Medicare. The cost side is real: open-ended federal subsidy spending, direct reinsurance payments to private insurers, and lower revenue for drug makers. The bill is a moderate-market-stabilization package rather than a single-payer plan, so it leaves the private insurance system largely intact around the new public option.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees in September 2017, sent to a Health Subcommittee three days later, and neither panel ever acted; it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Higgins of New York introduced the bill on September 12, 2017, joined by an initial list of 34 Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction, and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on September 15, 2017.
It eventually drew 50 cosponsors, all Democrats.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the rule shielding their Medicare prices from negotiation, and private insurers kept 50- to 64-year-olds in the individual market with no public buy-in competing against them. For ordinary people, nothing changed: pre-65 adults kept facing the individual market as it was, and cost-sharing subsidies and drug prices stayed as they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and private insurers

for.name: Rep. Brian Higgins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare buy-in and stabilization bill and recruited Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.role: Committees with jurisdiction over Medicare, drug pricing, and insurance markets
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.role: Republican-controlled House majority that controlled the floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor or scheduled it for consideration during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 50 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill never got committee or floor action.

industries.note: The bill repeals the statutory 'noninterference' rule and orders the government to negotiate Part D drug prices, directly cutting into drug company revenue on Medicare's largest drug benefit. Consumers and Medicare would capture the negotiated savings.

Insurers would lose 50- to 64-year-old customers to the Medicare buy-in and pay fees into the reinsurance fund, but would gain federal reinsurance payments for high-cost patients and reauthorized risk-corridor payments. The bill's stabilization pieces prop up the private market while the buy-in creates a public competitor for its oldest customers.

industries.industry: Health insurers on the ACA exchanges
industries.note: Reinsurance and risk corridors are built to keep private plans in the individual market and keep premiums down, preserving insurers' role as the coverage channel for people under 50, with the buy-in covering only the 50-64 band.
